me: Open-source framework for 3D FPGA generation with customizable vertical interconnects. Generates synthesizable RTL and produces complete bitstreams. Supports parametric exploration of 3D architectures.
nv: Open-source 3D FPGA framework with customizable vertical interconnects and end-to-end bitstream generation.
th: 3D FPGA design framework

t: Making the Best Switch: Encoding Strategy Management for Efficient TFHE Circuit Evaluation
pb: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (TFHE) circuit evaluation is computationally expensive. Different operations benefit from different plaintext encoding strategies, but selecting optimal strategies requires manual effort.
me: Synthesis framework that dynamically switches between plaintext encoding strategies during TFHE circuit evaluation. Strategy selection optimized per operation. Achieves 53.46% reduction in evaluation time.
nv: Dynamic encoding strategy switching for optimized TFHE circuit evaluation with automatic strategy selection.
th: TFHE encoding optimization

t: A Graph-Based Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework for Quantum Circuit Mapping with Look-Ahead Rewards and Biased Exploration
pb: Quantum circuit mapping requires inserting SWAP gates to match hardware topology constraints; minimizing additional gates is crucial to reduce circuit error rates in NISQ systems.
me: LARBE uses graph neural networks to encode quantum circuits and applies deep reinforcement learning with look-ahead rewards for trading immediate vs future benefits and biased exploration incorporating heuristic rules.
nv: Graph-based DRL framework with look-ahead rewards and biased exploration for quantum circuit mapping.
th: DRL-based quantum circuit mapping with look-ahead rewards

t: Seeing Through Designs: Attention-Based Knowledge Transfer for Preference-Guided Microarchitecture Search
pb: Microarchitecture design search faces large search spaces and lengthy validation flows; design knowledge reuse across architectures is limited by PPA metric discrepancies.
me: Uses cross-attention networks to capture microarchitectural topology and design tool configuration interdependencies for knowledge adaptation across architectures, complemented by uncertainty-guided optimization for preference-based search.
nv: Attention-based cross-architecture knowledge transfer with uncertainty-guided preference-based microarchitecture search.
th: Attention-based knowledge transfer for processor design search

t: CNOT Oriented Synthesis for Small-Scale Boolean Functions Using Spatial Structures of Parallelotopes
pb: Quantum circuit scalability is limited by gate fidelity and qubit counts in the NISQ era, restricting physical implementations to small-scale circuits. Existing logic network structures for quantum circuit synthesis neglect the spatial structure intrinsic to Boolean functions.
me: SSHR (Spatial Structure-based Hypercube Reduction) extracts global spatial features from parallelotopes embedded in hypercubes to minimize Multi-Control Toffoli gates. Two variants are introduced: SSHR-H uses heuristic functions to accelerate runtime, while SSHR-I integrates an Integer Linear Programming solver to maximize spatial structure utilization.
nv: Uses spatial structure of Boolean functions encoded by parallelotopes to access a broader optimization space for quantum circuit synthesis.
th: Quantum circuit optimization

t: SpecMamba: Accelerating Mamba Inference on FPGA with Speculative Decoding
pb: State Space Models (SSMs) like Mamba for long-sequence modeling on edge devices have autoregressive generation that remains memory-bound, and directly applying speculative decoding faces hidden state backtracking difficulties, tree-based parallel verification incompatibility, and hardware workload mismatch.
me: System-level memory-aware hybrid backtracking strategy coordinates draft and target models; algorithm-level FIFO-based tree verification with tiling minimizes memory access; hardware-level custom dataflow computes linear layers in parallel and SSM layers in series for maximal overlapping. Implemented on AMD FPGA platforms (VHK158 and VCK190).
nv: First FPGA-based accelerator for Mamba with speculative decoding combining system-algorithm-hardware co-design.
th: FPGA acceleration for SSMs

t: Apollo: Automated Routing-Informed Placement for Large-Scale Photonic Integrated Circuits
pb: Photonic integrated circuits (PICs) at scale are manually laid out due to analog custom layout nature, curvy waveguide structures, and single-layer routing resources with stringent physical constraints. Manual process takes weeks and is error-prone, fundamentally unscalable for large-scale PIC systems.
me: GPU-accelerated framework featuring asymmetric bending-aware wirelength function with explicit modeling of waveguide routing congestion and crossings; conditional projection gradually enforcing user-defined constraints (alignment, spacing); custom blockwise adaptive Nesterov-accelerated optimizer for stable, high-quality convergence. Tightly couples placement with physical-aware routing.
nv: First GPU-accelerated, routing-informed placement framework tailored for large-scale PICs coupling placement with physical-aware routing.
th: PIC design automation

t: Reconfigurable Stream Network Architecture
pb: FPGA-based DNN overlay accelerators suffer from layer-granularity serialization: von Neumann-style coarse-grained ISAs treat each layer instruction atomically, preventing dynamic layer fusion, inter-layer pipelining, and fine-grained bandwidth orchestration across heterogeneous resources (FPGA fabric + AI Engines).
me: RSN (Reconfigurable Stream Network) abstracts the datapath as a circuit-switched network of stateful functional units (FUs) connected by latency-insensitive data streams. Programming a computation means triggering a path through the FU network; multiple non-conflicting paths enable spatial and pipeline parallelism. A three-level instruction decoder fuses multiple FU uOP streams into a single RSN instruction stream with packet-level reuse to minimize instruction overhead (1 byte drives up to 1.6 GFLOPs). RSN-XNN, the prototype on Versal VCK190, virtualizes both FPGA BRAMs/DSPs and AI Engine tiles as heterogeneous FUs through a common stream interface, enabling dynamic sequential layer pipelining and fine-grained DDR/LPDDR bandwidth interleaving during phase transitions.
nv: RSN introduces a circuit-switched streaming network ISA abstraction that enables dynamic multi-layer pipelining and fine-grained bandwidth orchestration on FPGA overlays without per-layer bitstream reconfiguration—the first FPGA design to achieve this.

mx.speedup: 6.1x latency reduction for BERT vs. SOTA on VCK190; 2.4x–3.2x throughput for BERT/ViT/NCF/MLP
mx.energy_or_tops_w: 2.1x higher energy efficiency in FP32 vs. A100 at same 7nm node
mx.other: Matches T4 GPU latency with only 18% of its memory bandwidth

th: Circuit-switched streaming ISA for heterogeneous FPGA DNN overlays

t: Accelerating Simulation of Quantum Circuits under Noise via Computational Reuse
pb: Noisy quantum circuit simulation on HPC systems is prohibitively slow because simulators must iteratively re-execute nearly identical circuits thousands of times across different noise model trials, recomputing the same intermediate quantum states from scratch each time.
me: TQSim (Tree-Based Quantum Circuit Simulation) dynamically partitions a quantum circuit into subcircuits and constructs a tree of intermediate results that can be reused across different noisy simulation trials. The system identifies which subcircuit branches diverge due to noise injection and reuses cached intermediate density matrix or statevector results for the converging branches, avoiding redundant re-simulation. The approach is designed for multi-node distributed HPC setups with tight fidelity bounds on the approximation.
nv: Tree-based dynamic partitioning of quantum circuits enables reuse of intermediate quantum state results across noisy simulation trials, reducing total computation proportionally to reuse opportunities.

mx.speedup: up to 3.89x over Qulacs-based noisy simulator baseline

th: Tree-based intermediate result reuse for noisy quantum circuit simulation

t: Need for zkSpeed: Accelerating HyperPlonk for Zero-Knowledge Proofs
pb: Generating zero-knowledge proofs using the HyperPlonk zkSNARK protocol is prohibitively slow on CPUs, requiring minutes to hours, due to its four heterogeneous proof phases that demand large-bitwidth (255-381 bit) modular arithmetic over polynomials of degree up to 2^24. Existing ZKP accelerators target simpler protocols (Groth16, Orion, Spartan) that either require per-application trusted setups or produce large proofs, leaving HyperPlonk—which avoids both pitfalls—unaccelerated.
me: zkSpeed is a modular ASIC comprising eight dedicated hardware units: a unified SumCheck unit (handling ZeroCheck, PermCheck, and OpenCheck variants with shared modular multipliers across terms), an MSM unit based on Pippenger's algorithm with improved bucket aggregation reducing aggregation latency by 92%, a Multifunction Tree Unit (MTU) using hybrid DFS/BFS tree traversal for Build MLE, MLE Evaluate, and Product MLE, a FracMLE unit using constant-time Binary Extended Euclidean Algorithm (BEEA) with Montgomery batching (batch size 64) to amortize modular inversion costs, and an MLE Combine unit with resource sharing between sequential OpenCheck phases. Units communicate via a 4-channel shared bus; global SRAM stores compressed on-chip MLE tables (10-11x compression via binary packing), while streaming SumCheck computations flow through HBM (2 TB/s target). A full-chip simulator sweeps thousands of design configurations for Pareto-optimal area-performance tradeoffs.
nv: A unified SumCheck PE architecture that handles all three HyperPlonk SumCheck variants (ZeroCheck, PermCheck, OpenCheck) with shared modular multipliers—saving 48.9% area—combined with a novel hybrid DFS/BFS Multifunction Tree Unit and Montgomery-batched modular inversion pipeline that together cover the complete HyperPlonk proving protocol in a single ASIC.

mx.speedup: 801x geomean over AMD EPYC 7502 CPU at iso-compute area (366mm2, 2 TB/s HBM)
mx.other: 48.9% area saved on SumCheck PE via multiplier sharing; 92% reduction in MSM bucket aggregation latency; 41.6% area saved via Multifunction Tree unit reuse; 10-11x on-chip MLE compression

th: ASIC acceleration of zero-knowledge proof generation

t: FAST: An FHE Accelerator for Scalable-parallelism with Tunable-bit
pb: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) imposes enormous computational overhead compared to plaintext computation, and existing FHE accelerators do not exploit recent cryptographic optimizations—specifically hoisting technology and the gadget decomposition key-switching (KLSS) method—leaving significant performance on the table. Additionally, ciphertext level consumption varies significantly during application execution, causing workload imbalance that accelerators with fixed precision do not address.
me: FAST is an FHE accelerator that integrates hoisting technology (reducing redundant NTT operations in key-switching) and the KLSS gadget decomposition key-switching method. A versatile framework supports both hybrid and KLSS key-switching within a single application execution, dynamically adapting to varying ciphertext levels. The accelerator implements tunable-bit arithmetic to match the differing computational precision requirements of hybrid vs. KLSS key-switching at different ciphertext levels. Scalable parallelism is achieved through a configurable array of processing elements that can be provisioned to match the current workload's level and method requirements.
nv: A single FHE accelerator framework that simultaneously supports hoisting technology and both hybrid and KLSS gadget-decomposition key-switching methods with tunable-bit arithmetic, dynamically adapting to varying ciphertext level requirements within one application execution.

mx.speedup: Not stated in abstract (improved performance over prior FHE accelerators)
mx.other: Specific headline numbers not disclosed in abstract

th: FHE accelerator with hoisting and dual key-switching method support

t: Single Spike Artificial Neural Networks
pb: Standard ANNs require large-scale arithmetic with high energy consumption, while spiking neural networks (SNNs) circumvent this via biologically inspired computation but use fundamentally different algorithms from ANNs, preventing reuse of the mature ANN software stack and optimization techniques. The paper seeks an intermediate approach that achieves the energy efficiency of SNNs while remaining compatible with ANN algorithms and toolchains.
me: The design represents each ANN weight as a delay element and each activation magnitude as the arrival time of a digital signal. Complete ANNs are built on top of these temporal primitives through: (1) spatial and temporal reuse strategies enabling classical dataflows (e.g., weight-stationary) in a systolic array; (2) a noise-tolerant temporal summation operation for accumulation; (3) novel hybrid digital/temporal memory circuits for storing inter-layer activations; and (4) a temporal memory integration that manages activations between layers while preserving ANN algorithmic compatibility.
nv: Encoding ANN weights as delay elements and activation magnitudes as digital signal arrival times, enabling ANN-compatible systolic array dataflows on biologically inspired temporal circuits with 11x better energy than SNNs.

mx.energy_or_tops_w: 11x better energy vs SNNs; 3.5x better energy vs 8-bit digital systolic arrays
mx.accuracy: Inference accuracy evaluated across multiple MLPerf Tiny architectural parameter configurations

th: temporal-signal ANN execution for energy-efficient inference

t: Neo: Towards Efficient Fully Homomorphic Encryption Acceleration using Tensor Core
pb: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) imposes massive computational overhead—orders of magnitude over plaintext computation—that prevents practical deployment, while existing ASIC accelerators lack generality as FHE algorithms rapidly evolve. GPU-based solutions exist but fail to exploit tensor core (TCU) hardware for the dominant FHE primitives.
me: Neo maps the CKKS FHE scheme's core operations—Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) and polynomial multiplication—onto GPU Tensor Cores (TCUs) by reformulating them as matrix operations compatible with the TCU's INT8/FP16 matrix-multiply-accumulate pipeline. The design includes careful decomposition of NTT butterfly stages and residue number system (RNS) arithmetic to fit TCU matrix dimensions, with custom CUDA kernels orchestrating data layout, twiddle factor injection, and modular reduction to avoid overflow in low-precision arithmetic.
nv: Reformulating FHE polynomial arithmetic (NTT and RNS multiplication for CKKS) as tensor-core matrix operations, enabling use of specialized high-throughput TCU hardware for cryptographic workloads rather than general CUDA cores.

mx.other: Abstract truncated; headline numbers not available

th: tensor-core acceleration of FHE polynomial arithmetic

t: QR-Map: A Map-Based Approach to Quantum Circuit Abstraction for Qubit Reuse Optimization
pb: Identifying optimal qubit reuse opportunities in quantum circuits via mid-circuit measurements is NP-hard in the general case; existing frameworks either suffer from exponential search complexity or produce non-optimal results due to non-deterministic heuristics.
me: QR-Map abstracts computational dependencies by extracting and aligning two-qubit gates into a map structure, making dependency detection deterministic and tractable. The framework identifies qubit reuse opportunities by analyzing these aligned gate maps, ensuring qubit savings without introducing excessive idle time. It jointly optimizes gate serialization depth and crosstalk reduction, balancing circuit fidelity with hardware constraints through a deterministic, polynomial-time map-based search.
nv: A map-based circuit abstraction that aligns two-qubit gates to expose qubit reuse dependencies deterministically, replacing exponential DAG search with a structured, optimal qubit-reuse framework.

mx.accuracy: 20% average qubit reduction, 25% circuit depth reduction, 22% SWAP reduction vs state-of-the-art

th: Map-based qubit reuse optimization for quantum circuits

t: Reinforcement Learning-Guided Graph State Generation in Photonic Quantum Computers
pb: In photonic quantum computers (PQCs), generating graph states (entangled photon collections) requires finding an optimal generation sequence over quantum emitters, where three fidelity-critical metrics — generation time, number of emitters used, and number of CZ gates — are jointly minimized. Existing compilation frameworks either face exponential search complexity or fail to guarantee optimal results due to their non-deterministic properties.
me: RLGS (Reinforcement Learning-guided Graph State generation) frames the generation sequence problem as an RL optimization task. A map-based abstraction extracts and aligns two-qubit gate dependencies from quantum circuits into a structured representation, enabling the RL agent to detect dependency patterns and search for generation sequences that simultaneously reduce generation time, emitter count, and CZ gate insertions. The framework balances gate serialization depth against crosstalk reduction.
nv: RLGS uses a map-based circuit abstraction that converts generation sequence search from exponential dependency graph traversal into an RL-navigable state space, achieving joint optimization of all three fidelity metrics simultaneously.

mx.speedup: 31.1-57.5% reduction in generation time vs. state-of-the-art (small to large graph states)
mx.other: 13.9-17.5% emitter reduction; 37.7-57.8% CZ gate reduction

th: RL-guided compilation for photonic quantum graph state generation

t: LightML: A Photonic Accelerator for Efficient General Purpose Machine Learning
pb: General-purpose machine learning workloads require massive computational throughput that strains conventional electronic server infrastructure in terms of cost and power. Existing photonic computing proposals lack a complete system-level design with proper memory and buffer support to fully utilize the high-speed photonic crossbar.
me: LightML implements the first complete system-level photonic crossbar design for ML, pairing a photonic crossbar core with a carefully co-designed memory and buffer architecture that sustains greater than 80% utilization of the photonic crossbar. The system supports large-scale matrix-matrix multiplication (MMM), element-wise operations, non-linear activation functions, and convolutional layers via dedicated photonic and electronic functional units. The design targets both edge and data-center density profiles, delivering 325 TOP/s at 3 W.
nv: First system-level photonic crossbar design that includes a purpose-built memory and buffer architecture enabling sustained high utilization (>80%) of the photonic core across diverse ML operations.
th: photonic crossbar ML acceleration

t: Nyx: Virtualizing dataflow execution on shared FPGA platforms
pb: Existing multi-tenant FPGA virtualization systems support only task-parallel models, where distinct reconfigurable regions process independent data batches — this precludes dataflow execution (direct streaming between pipelined tasks), forcing dependent tasks to wait and incurring long end-to-end response times. No prior work supports dataflow pipelines in a virtualized, shared FPGA environment.
me: Nyx partitions the FPGA into distinct partially-reconfigurable regions and introduces virtual FIFOs — independent communication channels that decouple pipelined tasks from their predecessors and successors. When a task occupies one region, virtual FIFOs buffer inter-task data so that dependent tasks need not be co-scheduled simultaneously on the fabric. An FPGA hypervisor manages all data dependencies, tracks FIFO state, and dispatches pipelined tasks across regions at high throughput, enabling temporal multiplexing of dataflow pipelines across shared hardware.
nv: Virtual FIFOs that abstract inter-task communication channels, allowing pipelined dataflow tasks to execute independently across time-multiplexed FPGA regions without requiring simultaneous co-scheduling of all pipeline stages.

mx.speedup: 1.26x-8.87x throughput over state-of-the-art task-parallel virtualized FPGA; 2.8x-3.28x response time reduction in low-demand periods; 2x-2.75x in high-demand periods
mx.other: deadline violations reduced by up to 76.5% (low demand), 34.5% (high demand); tail response time reduced up to 1.9x

th: FPGA dataflow virtualization

t: Finesse: An Agile Design Framework for Pairing-based Cryptography via Software/Hardware Co-Design
pb: Pairing-based cryptography (PBC) accelerators require frequent re-engineering as security demands grow and pairing curve parameters evolve, but existing designs are either highly customized (inflexible) or flexible but low-performance, with no framework automating the algorithm-to-hardware translation across diverse pairing curves. The complex interdependency among algorithm choices, finite-field operator variants, and hardware configurations makes design-space exploration intractable manually.
me: Finesse introduces a three-layer abstraction: an intermediate representation (IR) for finite-field operations over arbitrary extension fields, a RISC-flavor Fp-level ISA with VLIW extension, and a parameterized hardware pipeline model. A specialized compiler performs SSA-based dataflow optimization, instruction scheduling with issue-slot affinity optimization, and register bank allocation before generating binary for target hardware. A cycle-accurate simulator enables co-design feedback loops with EDA toolchain synthesis metrics. The hardware implements modular arithmetic ALUs (mmul, madd, mlin, minv) in a multi-core SIMT architecture with shared instruction memory on ASIC (40 nm) and FPGA (Virtex-7) platforms.
nv: Issue-slot affinity scheduling that partitions pipeline slots into periodic intervals aligning Long (modmul) and Short (linear) instructions to eliminate write-back conflicts, combined with a co-design feedback loop between compiler and EDA synthesis for joint algorithm-architecture optimization across arbitrary pairing curves.

mx.area: 1.77 mm2 (1-core, 40nm); 8.00 mm2 (8-core, 40nm); 12.09 kops/mm2 vs 1.39 kops/mm2 for prior ASIC at 65nm equiv.
mx.ppa: 34x throughput, 6.2x slice efficiency vs FlexiPair; 3x throughput, 3.2x area efficiency vs SOTA ASIC
mx.other: Compilation time: 8.0s (BN254) to 53.1s (BLS24-509); IPC improved from 0.19 to 0.87-0.97

th: Agile compiler-driven co-design framework for pairing-based cryptography accelerators

t: Constant-Rate Entanglement Distillation for Fast Quantum Interconnects
pb: Existing quantum interconnect protocols cannot simultaneously achieve high fidelity and high rate of entanglement generation under realistic noisy local operations, creating a fundamental bottleneck for distributed quantum computing and blind quantum computation. Current entanglement distillation methods either have vanishing rate or fail to tolerate the noise levels present in physical systems.
me: The work develops a constant-rate entanglement distillation protocol using a sequence of two-way entanglement distillation rounds based on quantum error-detecting codes with increasing code rate. The scheme combines these iterated two-way distillation protocols with standard fault-tolerance techniques to achieve a net constant fraction of the raw entanglement pairs being converted to high-fidelity logical pairs. Numerical optimization is applied to minimize practical overhead given finite memory constraints.
nv: The first constant-rate (in expectation) entanglement distillation protocol for noisy quantum interconnects, achieved by chaining quantum error-detecting codes of increasing rate in a two-way distillation ladder.

mx.other: Constant-rate entanglement distillation demonstrated analytically and numerically; improvement over existing methods not quantified with specific numbers in the abstract

th: Constant-rate entanglement distillation for fault-tolerant quantum interconnects

t: Qtenon: Towards Low-Latency Architecture Integration for Accelerating Hybrid Quantum-Classical Computing
pb: Hybrid quantum-classical algorithms are bottlenecked by the decoupled architecture of current quantum hardware systems, which lacks low-latency communication channels and fine-grained software control for tightly coordinating quantum and classical computation. The high round-trip latency between host processor and quantum accelerator prevents real-time feedback loops required by variational algorithms.
me: Qtenon is a RISC-V extended chip implemented in Chisel that tightly couples classical and quantum processing via three hardware components: a unified memory hierarchy serving as a shared communication buffer between the host and quantum accelerators, an efficient quantum controller with dedicated data paths, and a multi-stage processing pipeline that exploits instruction-level parallelism across quantum-classical interaction phases. A custom ISA extension provides instructions for data communication, computation, fine-grained synchronization, and efficient scheduling of quantum-host interaction.
nv: Unified memory hierarchy bridging host and quantum accelerator combined with a custom RISC-V ISA extension enabling fine-grained synchronization and scheduling for hybrid quantum-classical algorithms in a tightly coupled chip.

mx.speedup: Up to 14.9x end-to-end speedup over state-of-the-art hybrid quantum-classical architectures

th: Tightly coupled quantum-classical processor architecture

t: ARTERY: Fast Quantum Feedback using Branch Prediction
pb: Quantum feedback in dynamic circuits introduces significant latency because each feedback branch must wait for measurement results to propagate through classical decoding and control, blocking gate execution and degrading circuit fidelity. The dynamic nature of mid-circuit measurement prevents speculative execution under current quantum control hardware.
me: ARTERY applies branch prediction to quantum feedback by combining two sources of information: historical statistics of branch outcomes and a real-time readout-pulse trajectory predictor that analyzes the in-flight pulse shape to predict the qubit state before full demodulation is complete. A reconciled branch predictor fuses these two signals to allow downstream gates to begin executing speculatively. Hardware support includes a scalable inter-FPGA backplane for feedback routing, a trigger mechanism for dynamic instruction timing, and an adaptive pulse sampling technique to maximize bandwidth.
nv: Applying classical branch prediction—fusing historical branch statistics with real-time readout-pulse trajectory analysis—to speculatively pre-execute quantum gates before mid-circuit measurement results are finalized.

mx.accuracy: Over 90% branch prediction accuracy; 1.24x fidelity improvement

th: Branch prediction for quantum feedback acceleration

t: HiPER: Hierarchically-Composed Processing for Efficient Robot Learning-Based Control
pb: Learning-Based Model Predictive Control (LMPC) for robot navigation combines neural network inference with iterative MPC optimization, creating a mixed workload with rapidly varying computational patterns that neither GPUs nor simple CPU-GPU integrations can serve efficiently. The workload alternates between dense ML computation and sparse, irregular MPC solves across time steps.
me: HiPER is a 1024-PE ASIC synthesized in 16nm CMOS (16.37 mm²) built around a fractal interconnect topology that nests local systolic arrays within a hierarchical extension to handle the traffic characteristics of LMPC. A six-level pointer queue hierarchy orchestrates program composition and execution, enabling temporal and spatial mapping of workload phases at runtime. The pointer queues serve as a lightweight control mechanism that composes heterogeneous sub-programs without a complex scheduler, allowing dynamic adaptation to workload changes.
nv: Fractal interconnect topology combining local systolic arrays with hierarchical extensions, orchestrated by a multi-level pointer queue hierarchy that enables runtime temporal and spatial remapping for mixed ML+MPC workloads.

mx.speedup: 10.75x over GTX 1080; 11.6x over RoboX; 22.2x over Plasticine
mx.energy_or_tops_w: 12.80x energy efficiency improvement over Jetson Orin Nano

th: ASIC accelerator for robot learning-based model predictive control

t: DS-TPU: Dynamical System for on-Device Lifelong Graph Learning with Nonlinear Node Interaction
pb: Electronic Dynamical System (DS) hardware achieves orders-of-magnitude speed and energy improvements over GNNs for graph inference via natural annealing, but it (1) lacks native on-device training support—forcing reliance on slower conventional hardware for model updates—and (2) restricts node interactions to linear functions, limiting expressiveness and training accuracy.
me: DS-TPU introduces two algorithmic-architectural co-design innovations. First, an on-device lifelong learning mechanism uses feedback electric current as a native loss signal in response to observed training data, enabling electron-speed model parameter refinement directly on the DS chip without off-chip software. Second, nonlinear DS node interactions are constructed from Chebyshev polynomial expansions, making the DS hardware compatible with the richer relational structure in graph data while remaining implementable in analog hardware. The DS-TPU architecture is evaluated at a 5-Watt power envelope on six real-world graph learning benchmarks.
nv: On-device lifelong learning via feedback electric current as a loss function, combined with Chebyshev polynomial nonlinear node interactions, enabling native training on an electronic Dynamical System chip.

mx.speedup: 810x over offline DS training on A100 GPU; 640x over GNN training on A100 GPU
mx.accuracy: 10.8% MAE reduction over best of five GNNs on six graph learning tasks

th: analog dynamical system chip with native on-device graph learning

t: IDEA-GP: Instruction-Driven Architecture with Efficient Online Workload Allocation for Geometric Perception
pb: Robotic geometric perception tasks (SLAM, Structure from Motion) involve diverse and dynamically varying computational operators — including point cloud registration, pose graph optimization, bundle adjustment, and feature matching — whose workload fluctuates with environment and task, preventing static mapping to specialized accelerators and causing poor resource utilization.
me: IDEA-GP is an FPGA-based instruction-driven accelerator built around an array of general-purpose computational units (PEs) optimized for spatial-positioning representations such as rotation matrices, quaternions, and homogeneous coordinates. A compiler performs online workload analysis — profiling operator types and sizes at runtime — and emits PE-targeted instructions to dynamically schedule and pipeline optimization sub-problems (e.g., least-squares solve, graph relaxation). This instruction-driven dispatch allows the same PE array to handle the varied compute patterns of SLAM (incremental pose estimation, loop closure) and SfM (bundle adjustment, triangulation) without hardware reconfiguration. The system is deployed on a Xilinx ZCU102 evaluation board.
nv: An instruction-driven online workload allocation compiler that dynamically schedules heterogeneous geometric-perception operators onto a unified PE array at runtime, achieving high resource utilization despite task and environment variability.

mx.speedup: 7.5x over Intel CPU and 19.7x over ARM CPU (SLAM); 16.4x over Intel CPU and 41.6x over ARM CPU (SfM) on Xilinx ZCU102

th: Instruction-driven FPGA accelerator for robotic geometric perception with online workload allocation

t: SwitchQNet: Optimizing Distributed Quantum Computing for Quantum Data Centers with Switch Networks
pb: In quantum data centers (QDCs), quantum processor units (QPUs) in different racks are interconnected via reconfigurable optical switch networks, and cross-rack quantum communications incur both long latency and dynamic switch reconfiguration delays, significantly increasing total circuit execution time and degrading quantum state fidelity.
me: SwitchQNet introduces a compiler that co-optimizes quantum communication scheduling at both the program layer (gate decomposition and qubit routing) and the network layer (optical switch reconfiguration scheduling). The compiler models the QDC network topology and switch reconfiguration latencies, then constructs a joint schedule that batches and reorders quantum gate communications to amortize switch reconfiguration overhead across multiple operations. The approach integrates with quantum error correction (QEC) to target fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC). The implementation is open-sourced at https://zenodo.org/records/15377656.
nv: A cross-layer compiler that jointly optimizes quantum gate scheduling and optical switch reconfiguration in quantum data centers, reducing end-to-end latency 8.02x over prior approaches by amortizing switch setup costs.

mx.other: Integrates with QEC for fault-tolerant quantum computing

th: Cross-layer compiler for quantum communication scheduling in optical-switch quantum data centers

t: Hardware-aware Calibration Protocol for Quantum Computers
pb: Quantum computer calibration—optimizing control parameters to ensure accurate gate implementation—does not account for physical qubit heterogeneity, and existing methods serialize calibration operations, causing excessive calibration overhead and suboptimal gate fidelity as qubit counts scale.
me: The protocol operates in two stages. First, a profiling phase evaluates qubit-pair responses to different waveform candidates, then assigns one of three calibration policies to each pair based on the profiling data (hardware-aware, fine-grained policy selection). Second, a graph-traversal algorithm identifies sets of compatible (non-interfering) calibration operations that can execute in parallel, converting the sequential calibration schedule into a parallel one. The protocol was validated on real IBM quantum hardware with up to 127 qubits.
nv: Fine-grained, per-qubit-pair waveform profiling that selects the best calibration policy per pair, combined with graph-traversal-based parallel scheduling, jointly reduces calibration time and two-qubit gate error simultaneously.

mx.accuracy: 1.84x reduction in median two-qubit gate error rate; 2.0-2.3x reduction in error per layered gate; 2x quantum volume improvement
mx.speedup: 8-25x reduction in total calibration overhead vs. sequential calibration; 2.12x additional reduction from profiling policy
mx.other: 1.26x reduction in pulse duration

th: hardware-aware parallel calibration protocol for quantum computers

t: S-SYNC: Shuttle and Swap Co-Optimization in Quantum Charge-Coupled Devices
pb: In Quantum Charge-Coupled Device (QCCD) trapped-ion architectures, coherent qubit shuttling across segmented electrode arrays increases thermal motion and consistently forces additional SWAP operations to restore qubit connectivity, significantly extending circuit execution time and degrading application success rates.
me: S-SYNC is a compiler that co-optimizes shuttle and SWAP counts simultaneously by exploiting QCCD-specific topology properties. It formulates QCCD routing as a static topology problem and incorporates generic SWAP gate insertion as a first-class operation alongside shuttle moves, rather than treating them independently. Scheduling heuristics then jointly minimize both operation types across the circuit, balancing the thermal motion cost of shuttling against the gate overhead of SWAPs. The compiler is evaluated across multiple QCCD topologies and initial qubit mapping strategies.
nv: Treating shuttle operations and SWAP insertions as co-equal, jointly-optimized variables in a static topology formulation—rather than as sequential, decoupled steps—reduces shuttling counts by 3.69x on average.

mx.accuracy: 1.73x average improvement in quantum application success rate

th: shuttle-SWAP co-optimization compiler for QCCD trapped-ion quantum processors

t: 6.8 A Real-Time Pixel-Compensated Source-Driver IC with Dual-Slope Error Detection and Multi-Channel Time-Multiplexing Compensator for Compact OLED Displays
pb: LTPS-TFT OLED displays suffer from pixel-to-pixel variations in DTFT parameters (Kp, Vth) and channel-wise voltage offsets (Vos), causing non-uniform drain current and luminance even with identical input data. Internal compensation via additional TFTs/capacitors reduces aperture ratio and efficiency.
me: A source-driver IC implements external real-time pixel compensation: (1) dual-slope error detection measures DTFT characteristics per pixel, (2) multi-channel time-multiplexed compensator dynamically adjusts Vdata for each pixel to correct current/luminance variation, (3) external approach preserves pixel aperture ratio vs. internal compensation.
nv: Dual-slope error detection + multi-channel time-multiplexed compensation enables per-pixel luminance correction without internal structural changes.
th: Per-pixel OLED display compensation via source-driver

t: 20.10 A 200GHz 200-Pixel 2D Near-Field Imager for Biomedical Applications
pb: Near-field mmWave/THz imaging systems face challenges: (1) single-source/single-detector-per-pixel limits resolution scalability, (2) lack of proper isolated resonator selection methods, (3) poor resonator Q at high frequencies near lossy biological samples, limiting sensitivity.
me: A 200GHz 200-pixel 2D near-field imager uses four key techniques: (1) Q-boosted Active Split-Ring Resonators (ASRR) enable dense pixel integration with individual selection via minimal capacitive loading, (2) selective pixel activation using shared source/detector (not per-pixel), (3) phase detection replaces power/frequency detection to avoid high free-running VCO phase noise, (4) correlated-doubling sampling (CDS) suppresses low-frequency noise.
nv: Q-boosted ASRR + phase detection enables true 2D scalable near-field imagers with high sensitivity despite lossy biological samples.
th: Scalable THz near-field imager with Q-boosted resonators

t: A Compact 10b Source Driver IC with Delta-Sigma Pulse Width Modulation for Low-Voltage Digital Interpolation Achieving 1884μm2/Channel
pb: High-resolution mobile displays require more source-driver channels, increasing silicon area and cost. Conventional interpolation sub-DAC topologies (Gm-adjustment, switched-capacitor, charge-modulation) suffer from inherent nonlinearity (Gm methods) or require additional capacitors/high-voltage devices that increase channel area.
me: A 10-bit compact source-driver IC uses delta-sigma pulse-width-modulation (SD-PWM) for low-voltage digital interpolation between gamma voltages. SD-PWM replaces analog interpolation circuits with digital modulation, reducing capacitor and transistor overhead while maintaining linearity.
nv: Delta-sigma PWM interpolation enables compact low-voltage DAC without capacitors or high-voltage blocks, achieving 1884μm²/channel.
th: Compact SD-PWM source-driver IC for high-resolution displays

t: 20.6 Fully Integrated Self-Propelling Microrobot in 180nm CMOS with Sub-GHz Parity-Time-Symmetry On-Chip Energy Harvesting and Traveling Wave Electroosmosis Actuation
pb: Autonomous motion integration remains challenging on CMOS dies—prior designs integrate energy harvesting and control, but either rely on lossy magnetic resonance coupling or require specialized photovoltaic fabrication processes incompatible with standard CMOS.
me: This design integrates parity-time-symmetry energy harvesting operating at sub-GHz frequencies with traveling-wave electroosmosis actuation mechanisms on a single CMOS die. The approach uses on-chip electroosmotic channels to generate propulsion forces directly from the harvested energy, eliminating the need for external actuation components or highly sensitive power coupling schemes.
nv: First demonstration of fully integrated sub-GHz parity-time-symmetry energy harvesting coupled directly to electroosmotic actuation for autonomous microrobot motion, all on a single 180nm CMOS die.
th: Self-contained microrobot with integrated energy harvesting and electroosmotic actuation

t: 11.4 A Gm-C RF Quadrature-Current-Generation Technique with 40dB IRR in 0.65V 2mW Multi-Mode CMOS GNSS Receiver
pb: Signal-quadrature receiver topologies offer power efficiency over LO-quadrature designs but suffer from poor I/Q phase and amplitude accuracy due to parasitic capacitances and impedances that are difficult to calibrate when using signal-engaged switches.
me: A Gm-C (transconductance-capacitive) RF quadrature-current-generation technique that derives orthogonal I and Q signals directly from the RF signal using transconductor circuits rather than passive switches. This approach reduces parasitic sensitivity and enables robust phase/amplitude balance calibration.
nv: Gm-C based quadrature generation achieving 40 dB image-rejection ratio (IRR) in a signal-quadrature topology, eliminating phase/amplitude imbalance challenges of conventional switch-based quadrature approaches.
th: Ultra-low-power Gm-C quadrature receiver for multi-mode GNSS applications

t: An Easy-Drive 16MS/s Pipelined-SAR ADC Using Split Coarse-Fine Input-Buffer-Sampling Scheme and Fast Robust Background Inter-Stage Gain Calibration
pb: Pipelined-SAR ADCs suffer from two practical challenges: (1) large sampling capacitance for noise suppression makes the input difficult to drive at medium speeds (1–20 MS/s), requiring either high supply voltage or complex predictors; (2) energy-efficient dynamic amplifiers suffer from inter-stage gain variation under PVT conditions, requiring fast and robust background calibration.
me: A 16 MS/s pipelined-SAR ADC using a split coarse-fine input-buffer-sampling scheme that relaxes sampling-capacitor voltage slew requirements, enabling operation from 1.8/0.9 V dual supplies without external drivers. A fast, PVT-robust background gain-calibration technique uses offset cancellation and a metastability detector with probability control, with 2-bit input dithering to ensure convergence across varying input conditions.
nv: Split coarse-fine input-buffer sampling scheme eliminating the need for external driving circuits or high supply voltage, combined with fast metastability-based background calibration robust across PVT.
th: Easy-drive pipelined-SAR ADC with split buffer sampling and fast background calibration

t: 4.4 A 0.36nW/0.9V 32kHz Crystal Oscillator Using Analog Regulation for Cross-Current Avoidance
pb: Ultra-low-power 32 kHz crystal oscillators typically require supply voltages >0.5 V to minimize switching losses in inverter-based circuits; recent pulsed-injection techniques achieve lower power but require additional regulation circuitry that isn't included in energy budgets, and don't operate efficiently from standard battery supply voltages (0.9–2 V).
me: A 32 kHz crystal oscillator using analog regulation for cross-current avoidance that operates directly from 0.9–2 V supply without intermediate regulation. The sustaining amplifier uses novel regulation concepts to minimize inverter switching losses by reducing unwanted cross-currents, shifting loss-suppression from voltage domain to time domain without requiring separate power supplies.
nv: First 32 kHz XO achieving sub-0.5 nW power consumption at 0.9 V supply through analog regulation, operating directly from battery voltage without external regulation circuitry.
th: Ultra-low-power 32 kHz crystal oscillator with analog regulation for battery-powered IoT

t: SPAD Flash LiDAR with Chopped Analog Counter for 76m Range and 120klx Background Light
pb: Flash LiDAR using single-photon avalanche diodes (SPADs) must simultaneously achieve long range (76m), high depth resolution, and high frame rates under strong background light (120klx) without performance degradation.
me: Direct time-of-flight (dToF) sensor using SPADs with chopped analog counter architecture that suppresses background-light interference and enables 76m range with high frame-rate histogramming at 120klx ambient light.
nv: Chopped analog counter design enabling robust dToF sensing under extreme background-light conditions (120klx) while achieving practical 76m range.
th: Background-light-robust flash LiDAR via SPADs.

t: 20.7 A 384-Site Chip Platform for Biochemical Applications with Individual Site Precision Temperature Control
pb: Biochemical processors require independent temperature control on multiple sites (384-site platform) for parallel PCR, gene assembly, and other thermally-tuned reactions, but silicon substrate thermal conductivity prevents efficient local isolation and precise sensing.
me: 384-site chip platform using thermal isolation structures and independent local temperature sensors/heaters per site, overcoming substrate thermal conductivity to achieve precise individual-site temperature control for biochemical applications.
nv: Monolithic 384-site platform with per-site independent temperature control achieved via substrate engineering to prevent thermal cross-talk.
th: Multi-site biochemical processor with independent thermal zones.

t: 25.1 A Physics-Inspired Oscillator-Based Mixed-Signal Optimization Engine for Solving 50-Variable 218-Clause 3-SAT Problems with 100% Solvability and 31.7μs Solution Time
pb: Boolean satisfiability (SAT) solving is NP-complete; existing hardware solvers are limited to small problem sizes (<20 variables), suffer from long solution times (ms-level), or require complex problem embedding with high preprocessing overhead.
me: Physics-inspired oscillator-based mixed-signal optimization engine mapping 3-SAT problems to coupled-spin dynamical systems with continuous-time operation and massive parallelism, achieving 100% solvability on 50-variable, 218-clause 3-SAT instances in 31.7μs.
nv: Oscillator-based spin system design achieving 50-variable 3-SAT solvability without complex embedding preprocessing, using all-to-all connected problem mapping.
th: Oscillator-based analog SAT solver.

t: 23.5 MAE: A 3nm 0.168mm2 576MAC Mini AutoEncoder with Line-Based Depth-First Scheduling for Generative AI in Vision on Edge Devices
pb: Deploying generative vision models (diffusion) on edge devices requires running autoencoders efficiently within tight area/power budgets; limited on-chip memory forces high DRAM access (40–80% of energy cost) and on-chip memory constraints cause temporal under-utilization of MAC units.
me: MAE is a 3nm domain-specific tiny NPU integrating 576 MACs in 0.168 mm² using line-based depth-first fusion with branch-handling to minimize external memory access (EMA). Local H-reuse caching exploits inter-layer data locality; direct links bypass redundant dataflow stages. Global scheduling framework optimizes latency and EMA jointly across the autoencoder graph.
nv: Line-based depth-first fusion combined with H-reuse caching and optimized scheduling reduces DRAM access by 40–80% vs. layer-by-layer approaches on tiny autoencoders.

mx.other: 576 MACs, 40–80% EMA reduction vs. layer-by-layer

th: Domain-specific NPU for edge generative vision

t: 26.2 A Wideband Replicas-Rejection Digital Transmitter Using Joint-Digital-Analog Interpolation and Filtering in 28nm CMOS
pb: Wideband digital transmitters (DTXs) struggle with sampling replicas at f_LO + n×f_s that fall close to signal band, violating emission masks and requiring high sampling rates + expensive off-chip RF filters. Supporting multiple sub-6 GHz standards (LB/HB) forces separate RF chains, increasing area and complexity.
me: Joint digital-analog interpolation and filtering strategy: optimized digital polyphase filter reduces per-channel sampling rate while maintaining high output rate; wideband quadrature DPA with IQ-cell-sharing and transformer-based load modulation; analog interpolation integrated into DPA circuit to suppress replicas. Unified architecture eliminates need for separate LB/HB chains.
nv: Co-design of digital polyphase filtering + analog interpolation within DPA suppresses sampling replicas without high-speed off-chip filtering, enabling single unified wideband DTX.

mx.other: Wideband coverage, replica suppression, area/power reduction vs. separate chains

th: Joint digital-analog DTX for wideband sub-6 GHz

t: 9.5 A Sub-1V, 50mV Dropout LDO Using Pseudo-Impedance Buffer with Phase-Margin Improvement Design
pb: Sub-1V analog LDOs face conflicting requirements: must supply heavy load currents (I_L) while maintaining stability under light load without Miller compensation. Current-mirror (CM) buffers used in prior designs cannot cover wide load ranges—high K ratios enable heavy I_L but degrade light I_L performance (buffer resistance increases, shifting gate pole to low frequency).
me: Pseudo-impedance buffer replaces conventional current-mirror buffer, decoupling buffer resistance from load current dependency. Frequency-compensation strategy improves phase margin across the load range without requiring high-order compensation. Single-stage error amplifier + pseudo-impedance buffer + pass transistor structure avoids Miller compensation, maintaining stability at sub-1V.
nv: Pseudo-impedance buffer enables wide load-current coverage (light to heavy) in sub-1V LDO without load-dependent phase margin degradation.

mx.other: Sub-1V operation, 50 mV dropout, wide load current range

th: Sub-1V LDO with wide-load pseudo-impedance buffer

t: A 3.47 NEF 175.2dB FOMs Direct Digitization Front-End Featuring Delta Amplification for Enhanced Dynamic Range and Energy Efficiency in Bio-Signal Acquisition
pb: Bio-signal acquisition (EEG, ExG) requires low input-referred noise (~50–60 nV/√Hz) but must reject large artifacts (100+ mV stimulation artifacts). Conventional LNA-based front-ends saturate under artifacts and require seconds to recover; ADC-first VCO-based DSM approaches achieve wide dynamic range but suffer 80–120 nV/√Hz noise (vs. 50–60 nV/√Hz requirement), due to noise-linearity tradeoff in first integrator.
me: ADC-first direct digitization using delta amplification in the first integrator improves noise-linearity tradeoff. Delta amplifier topology extends linear input range while maintaining low NEF (noise efficiency factor). VCO-based DSM provides inherent dynamic range without frontend gain, enabling high artifact rejection (100+ mV) while meeting low-noise specs.
nv: Delta amplification in ADC-first VCO-DSM simultaneously achieves 3.47 NEF (low noise) and enhanced dynamic range for bio-signal artifact rejection.

mx.other: NEF 3.47, FoMs 175.2 dB, IRN 50–60 nV/√Hz, dynamic range >100 mV

th: Low-noise, high-DR bio-signal front-end

t: 9.10 A 93%-Peak-Efficiency Battery-Input 12-to-36V-Output Inductor-in-the-Middle Hybrid Boost Converter with Continuous Input and Output Currents and Fast Transient with No RHP Zero
pb: Conventional boost converters face challenges in high voltage conversion ratios with very short turn-on pulses, significant voltage stress on inductors and transistors, and inherent right-half-plane zero that limits transient response speed.
me: Proposes a hybrid inductor-in-the-middle topology that reduces voltage stress on components, mitigates the RHP zero issue, and enables faster transient response while maintaining continuous input and output currents for improved efficiency and reliability.
nv: Inductor-in-the-middle architecture eliminating the RHP zero limitation and reducing voltage stress across power switches in high-ratio boost conversion.
th: High-efficiency hybrid boost converter for emerging edge applications

t: A Rectifier-Less Piezoelectric Energy-Harvesting Interface with a Sense & Track MPPT Achieving Single-Cycle Convergence and 568% Shock Power Improvement
pb: Existing piezoelectric energy harvesting (PEH) systems with bias-flip rectifiers and MPPT perform well under periodic vibrations but degrade sharply under shock conditions due to slow impedance-matching speed for fast amplitude variations.
me: Rectifier-less interface with sense & track (SST) MPPT algorithm converges to maximum power point in a single vibration cycle, enabling rapid impedance matching for any vibration amplitude via analog tracking without traditional rectifier losses.
nv: Single-cycle MPPT convergence using rectifier-less architecture and SST algorithm to match fast-varying shock inputs.
th: Fast-adaptive piezoelectric energy harvesting for edge IoT

t: 21.6 A 2A Fully Analog Distribution LDO with Noise Immunity for an SoC
pb: Analog distribution LDOs (DISLDOs) for SoCs suffer from noise coupling on analog control signals between distributed power transistors, resulting in excessive output voltage ripple and preventing practical deployment in advanced SoCs.
me: A fully analog DISLDO design incorporates noise-immune analog signal distribution and transmission techniques to maintain even current distribution across power transistors despite high on-chip noise, achieving 2A output current with stable regulation.
nv: Noise-immune analog control signal distribution enabling practical analog DISLDOs in noisy SoC environments.
th: Noise-immune analog distribution LDO for SoCs

t: 12.2 p-Circuits: Neither Digital Nor Analog
pb: Traditional analog and digital circuits present inherent trade-offs in power, area, and performance; a new computing paradigm is needed that combines benefits of both without requiring ADC/DAC conversions.
me: p-circuits introduce a probabilistic computing model where circuit inputs and outputs maintain digital-like interfaces (no ADC/DAC), but the output is a random binary variable whose probability P(B=1) is governed by an analog function A(inputs) that continuously varies between 0 and 1. This enables stochastic computation where probability encodes information.
nv: Probabilistic circuit paradigm (p-circuits) using analog probability functions as a computational substrate without digital-analog conversion overhead.

mx.other: Probabilistic computation without ADC/DAC

th: Probabilistic circuits bridging analog and digital computation

t: 2.9 STEP: An 8K-60fps Space-Time Resolution-Enhancement Neural-Network Processor for Next-Generation Display and Streaming
pb: Rendering 8K-UHD 60fps videos on edge devices requires balancing model depth for quality against resource constraints, and managing on-chip memory overhead from deformable convolution with modulation (DCM) across multiple temporal alignment layers.
me: The processor implements a space-time video super-resolution (STVSR) algorithm with layer-fusion (LF) workflow to reduce intermediate feature map storage, deformable convolution for temporal alignment across frames, and a PE array architecture sized for 8K-60fps throughput while minimizing power consumption.
nv: Layer-fusion workflow that reduces on-chip memory overhead from deformable convolution modulation by fusing operations across multiple temporal alignment layers.
th: 8K video super-resolution on edge devices

t: 20.9 An Autonomous and Lightweight Microactuator Driving System Using Flying Solid-State Batteries
pb: Small-scale flying electromechanical systems (microrobotics) require efficient high-voltage drive systems for electrostatic and piezoelectric actuators while meeting stringent weight (<1-2g) and power constraints for flight endurance (10s of minutes).
me: The system manages reactive energy delivery to capacitive loads by using flying solid-state batteries that enable integrated power conversion from low-voltage sources (3-5V) to high voltages (tens of volts), optimizing the voltage conversion ratio and reactive power efficiency.
nv: Flying solid-state battery integration for autonomous lightweight high-voltage power conversion in microrobotics applications.
th: Lightweight microactuator drive for flying robots

t: 17.2 A 28nm 4.05µJ/Encryption 8.72kHMul/s Reconfigurable Multi-Scheme Fully Homomorphic Encryption Processor for Encrypted Client-Server Computing
pb: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables privacy-preserving machine learning but incurs prohibitive power consumption and fabrication costs for bootstrapping operations; supporting multiple FHE schemes (BGV, BFV, CKKS) and diverse client/server primitives while managing intensive memory bottlenecks remains challenging.
me: The 28nm FHE processor implements reconfigurable architecture supporting BGV, BFV, and CKKS schemes with optimized primitives for both client and server computation patterns; architecture-circuit co-optimizations address (I)NTT and polynomial automorphism overhead while managing on-chip data movement.
nv: First silicon-proven reconfigurable multi-scheme FHE processor supporting both client-side and server-side encrypted computation patterns with integrated memory optimization.
th: Reconfigurable FHE processor for privacy-preserving ML

t: 25.4 A Micromachined Heterogeneously Integrated Active-Probe Enabling Non-Disruptive In-Situ Measurements from DC to 50GHz
pb: Debugging and failure analysis of densely integrated microsystems require probing at tight pitches with minimal signal distortion, but traditional 50Ω test equipment introduces excessive capacitive and inductive loading at microscale interfaces.
me: Micromachined probe substrate heterogeneously integrated with high-performance RF sense amplifier; high-Z probe design minimizes capacitive/inductive loading at test point, while integrated sense amp enables low-noise signal acquisition from DC to 50GHz.
nv: Heterogeneous integration of micromachined probe with on-probe RF sense amp eliminates external 50Ω test equipment bottleneck, enabling non-disruptive, high-Z probing at microsystem interfaces.

mx.other: DC-to-50GHz measurement bandwidth, non-disruptive probing at microsystem pitch

th: Active heterogeneous-integrated probe for high-speed microsystem debugging

t: 28.4 A 143dB-Dynamic-Range 119dB-CMRR Capacitance-to-Digital Converter for High-Resolution Floating-Target Displacement Sensing
pb: Capacitive displacement sensors for nanomechatronic systems are susceptible to high-frequency electric-field interference on electrically floating targets, requiring rejection of both low-frequency and high-frequency noise while maintaining high dynamic range (up to 500pF).
me: Phase-Domain-Delta-Sigma modulator (PD-ΔΣM) converts sensing capacitance to phase shift via lowpass RC front-end, then digitizes with high-resolution modulator. Inherent filtering in front-end/readout circuits provides dual-band noise rejection: 119dB CMRR near DC, 97dB around 100MHz, achieving 143dB dynamic range (35.2aF–500pF) without sub-ranging.
nv: Phase-domain delta-sigma modulation architecture providing simultaneous high dynamic range and dual-band common-mode rejection without sub-ranging complexity.
th: high-dynamic-range noise-immune capacitance-to-digital conversion

t: A 4.6μW 3.3-NEF Biopotential Amplifier with 133VPP Common-Mode Interference Tolerance and 102dB Total Common-Mode Rejection Ratio for Two-Electrode Recording System
pb: Two-electrode biopotential recording (EEG/ECG) systems experience large common-mode interference (>100V_PP) from power-source coupling via parasitic body and ground capacitances. Traditional CMI cancellation (charge-pump based) tolerates only ~20V_PP and adds noise; CM-averaging approaches ignore parasitic ground capacitance (C_GND), making them unsuitable for realistic ground-isolated systems.
me: Novel architecture addressing C_GND parasitic capacitance: ground-isolated system with displacement current splitting between body (C_Body) and ground (C_GND). Technique maintains high input impedance (Z_IN-CM-C) while providing 102dB total CMRR and 133V_PP CMI tolerance. Low-power design achieves 4.6μW with noise efficiency factor (NEF) of 3.3, enabling precise differential biopotential measurement despite massive CM voltages.
nv: High-CMRR AFE explicitly accounting for parasitic ground capacitance in ground-isolated recording, achieving 133V_PP CMI tolerance at ultra-low power with minimal noise.
th: ultra-low-power high-CMRR biopotential AFE with parasitic C_GND compensation

t: 7.4 A 112Gb/s DSP-Based PAM-4 Receiver with an LC-Resonator-Based CTLE for >52dB Loss Compensation in 4nm FinFET
pb: High-speed wireline transceivers (100Gb/s+) for AI/GPU interconnects and PCIe 7.0 require signal recovery over long channels with severe channel loss (>52dB). Traditional Continuous-Time Linear Equalization (CTLE) struggles with high-loss channels; existing DSP-based receivers lack energy-efficient, broadband equalization architectures.
me: DSP-based 112Gb/s PAM-4 receiver with novel LC-resonator-based CTLE providing >52dB loss compensation. Architecture combines: (1) LC-resonator front-end achieving broadband peaking/gain without power-hungry analog inductors; (2) DSP backend for adaptive equalization and PAM-4 symbol detection; (3) latency reduction techniques (analog data path optimization) minimizing overall receive latency. 4nm FinFET implementation achieves energy efficiency suitable for data-center deployment.
nv: LC-resonator-based CTLE enabling >52dB loss compensation in energy-efficient DSP-based PAM-4 receiver.
th: LC-resonator CTLE for energy-efficient extreme-loss PAM-4 reception

t: 33.3 A 125-to-170GHz Power-Efficient Phase Shifter in SiGe BiCMOS with Outphasing Gain and Phase Corrections
pb: Sub-THz phased-array transceivers for high-resolution radar and wireless communications require broadband, power-efficient phase shifters spanning 125–170GHz. Traditional phase-shifter architectures struggle with phase accuracy, amplitude imbalance, and power efficiency at such high frequencies in silicon technologies.
me: Power-efficient phase shifter leveraging outphasing technique for simultaneous gain and phase correction. Outphasing decomposes phase-amplitude modulation into orthogonal constant-amplitude paths, enabling efficient RF amplification with minimal power. Integrated gain adjustment and phase correction compensate for process/temperature variations. SiGe BiCMOS technology provides high-frequency performance suitable for 125–170GHz operation while maintaining integration density.
nv: Outphasing-based phase shifter with integrated gain and phase correction achieving power efficiency at sub-THz frequencies.
th: power-efficient outphasing phase shifter for sub-THz phased arrays

t: 5.9 A 21-to-31 GHz DPD-Less Quadrature RFDAC with Invariant Impedance and Scalable LO Leakage
pb: RF digital-to-analog converters (RFDACs) for mm-wave wireless transmitters (high-order QAM, wideband modulation) suffer nonlinearity increasing with frequency due to: (1) varied output impedance across unit array vs. baseband code, (2) distributed parasitics, (3) LO leakage. Existing solutions—DPD (complex, frequency-dependent), open-loop linearization (PVT-variant), self-calibration (loop-response-limited)—are inadequate; extra bits added for intrinsic nonlinearity compensation waste power in high-GS/s baseband.
me: DPD-less broadband mm-wave RFDAC (21–31GHz) with two key innovations: (1) invariant output impedance design ensuring unit-cell impedance independence from baseband code, eliminating impedance-induced nonlinearity; (2) scalable LO-leakage suppression technique adaptively reducing LO feedthrough across PVT conditions without feedback loops. Architecture achieves inherent linearity suitable for high-order QAM without requiring complex DPD, open-loop adaptation, or calibration loops.
nv: Intrinsically linear RFDAC with invariant impedance and adaptive LO-leakage suppression eliminating DPD requirement.
th: intrinsically linear DPD-less mm-wave RFDAC with invariant impedance

t: 1.2 From Chips to Thoughts: Building Physical Intelligence into Robotic Systems
pb: Generative AI deployment in robotics and edge systems faces high energy costs for both training and inference on large multi-modal models, constraining real-time autonomous system deployment.
me: Physical intelligence architecture for robotic systems integrating energy-efficient AI computation, sensorimotor feedback, and real-time control through optimized chip design and system-level power management.
nv: Integration of generative AI with embodied robotic control, addressing the energy-efficiency gap between datacenter models and edge deployment.
th: energy-efficient AI for robotic physical intelligence

t: 13.5 An 18.5µW/qubit Cryo-CMOS Charge-Readout IC Demonstrating QAM Multiplexing for Spin Qubits
pb: Scaling spin qubits to thousands of devices requires simultaneous readout with minimal per-qubit power consumption and footprint, but existing FDM reflectometry and integrator schemes are limited by bulky inductors or poor scaling to large arrays.
me: Cryo-CMOS charge-readout IC using quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM) multiplexing to read multiple spin qubits on a single carrier frequency, eliminating bulky inductors via capacitive-feedback transimpedance amplifier architecture.
nv: QAM multiplexing for frequency-domain spin qubit readout, enabling multiple qubits per carrier frequency instead of one qubit per carrier in prior OOK schemes.
th: scalable cryo-CMOS spin qubit readout with QAM multiplexing

t: 3.3 A Passive Switched-Capacitor-Based Multimode Amplifier with a Logarithmic Conformity Error of 0.75% from -25 to 200°C
pb: Harsh geothermal and high-temperature environments (up to 200°C) require sensor front-end amplifiers with wide dynamic range (>80dB), low temperature drift, and accurate phase/amplitude across extreme temperature spans. Existing logarithmic amplifiers exhibit high temperature dependence; low-drift amplifiers require complex trimming and compensation.
me: A passive switched-capacitor (SC) topology with multimode operation achieves high dynamic range and temperature stability. The design leverages discrete-time SC amplification to improve noise efficiency while avoiding the thermal drift issues of traditional logarithmic or low-drift amplifiers, using novel compensation mechanisms for stability across -25 to 200°C.
nv: Passive switched-capacitor multimode amplifier achieving 0.75% logarithmic conformity error across -25 to 200°C without requiring trimmed ratios or complex temperature compensation circuits.

mx.other: Temperature range: -25 to 200°C, DR >80dB

th: High-temperature sensor amplification via passive switched-capacitor topology

t: 13.3 A Cryo-BiCMOS Controller for 9Be+-Trapped-Ion-Based Quantum Computers
pb: Trapped-ion quantum computers require cryogenic control electronics operating at ~4K to interface with ion traps; existing digital controllers consume excessive power and limit qubit scalability.
me: Cryo-BiCMOS (bipolar + CMOS) controller operating at 4K for trapped-ion systems; leverages bipolar transistors' superior low-temperature performance and CMOS for integration. Implements quantum-charge-coupled-device (QCCD) control for ion shuttling and entanglement operations.
nv: First integrated cryo-BiCMOS controller enabling scalable trapped-ion quantum computing with QCCD architecture.
th: Cryo-BiCMOS control for scalable trapped-ion quantum computers

t: 27.4 A BJT-Based Temperature Sensor with an 80fJ.K2 Resolution FoM
pb: BJT-based temperature sensors require high energy efficiency while maintaining high accuracy; existing designs using resistor-based sensors or CT-ΔΣM approaches consume more power or occupy larger area.
me: NPN-based temperature sensor using noise-optimized charge-balancing continuous-time ΔΣ modulator (CTΔΣM) to digitize PTAT and CTAT current ratio. Current-assisted amplifier improves conversion gain while maintaining low noise.
nv: Charge-balancing CTΔΣM with noise-optimized design and current-assisted amplifier achieving 2.5x better energy efficiency than state-of-the-art.
th: Energy-efficient BJT temperature sensor via noise-optimized CTΔΣM

t: A 4GS/s Fully Analog 256×256 MP-Based Cross-Correlator with 1000TOPS/W Compute Efficiency and 1.3TOPS/mm2 Compute Density in 22nm SOI CMOS
pb: Multi-lag cross-correlation (X-Corr) is essential for radar range/velocity detection and communication synchronization; traditional digital approaches (ADC + MACs) achieve only 5–20 TOPS/W; analog approaches require on-chip delays and multiple correlators causing large area/power overhead.
me: Fully-analog 256×256 cross-correlator using margin-propagation (MP) based four-transistor analog compute cells. Sampling-based approach creates large analog delays on-chip without dedicated delay-line area. Single-shot readout across all 256 X-Corr lags via MP propagation.
nv: Margin-propagation (MP) analog compute cell achieving 256-length X-Corr with high efficiency (996–1060 TOPS/W) and compute density (1.3 TOPS/mm^2).

mx.speedup: 6.6x vs. prior analog, orders-of-magnitude vs. digital ADC+MAC

th: Ultra-efficient fully-analog multi-lag cross-correlator for radar/communications

t: 2.3 Granite Rapids-D: Intel Xeon 6 SoC for vRAN, Edge, Networking, and Storage
pb: vRAN (virtualized radio access networks), edge servers, networking, and storage workloads have diverging requirements: compute-optimized SKUs need scalar/data-parallel performance with low-latency high-bandwidth memory; edge SKUs require rugged operation (-40°C to 85°C) with dynamic temperature support.
me: Granite Rapids-D (GNR-D): Intel Xeon 6 SoC offering dual optimization strategies: (1) compute-optimized SKU with high scalar/parallel throughput, PCIe5, low-latency memory for data-center edge and vRAN; (2) edge-optimized SKU rated for rugged -40°C to 85°C operation with full dynamic range thermal support. Integrated confidential AI security (TEE) and ethernet/accelerator support across both classes.
nv: Dual-SKU strategy targeting both high-performance edge and rugged-environment deployment in single SoC family.
th: Flexible dual-SKU SoC for edge compute and vRAN

t: 18.8 A Cryo-CMOS 800MS/s 7b CI-SAR with only 4fF Input Capacitance and 64dB SFDR
pb: Quantum qubit readout circuits (transmon, spin qubits, gate-based) consume 10–108mW total system power; ADC driver (LNA, mixer, filters) dominates power budget at ~90% of total, while SAR ADCs themselves consume only ~10% but still require high-impedance inputs to avoid driver power escalation.
me: Charge-injection SAR ADC (CI-SAR) with exceptionally low input capacitance (4fF) via dedicated charge-injection DAC. Exploits cryo-CMOS (40nm bulk CMOS at 6.5K) property that kT/C noise becomes negligible, enabling tiny capacitors. 7-bit resolution at 800MS/s with 64.1dB SFDR.
nv: Charge-injection DAC maximally exploiting low kT/C noise at cryogenic temperatures to achieve record-low input capacitance (4fF).
th: Ultra-low-input-capacitance cryo-CMOS ADC for quantum qubit readout

t: 7.9 A 60Gb/s NRZ Burst-Mode CDR with Cross-Injection Locking and Flash Phase Detector Achieving 0.13ns Reconfiguration Time in 28nm CMOS
pb: Rapidly reconfigurable photonic switch networks operating at ns-scale require burst-mode clock and data recovery (BM-CDR) with sub-ns reconfiguration time, but prior injection-locking BM-CDRs suffer from poor jitter at higher data rates.
me: 60Gb/s burst-mode CDR using cross-injection-locking technique to suppress recovered-clock jitter, combined with a flash phase detector (PD) that extracts phase information between data and sampling clock within 2UI, achieving 0.13ns reconfiguration time in 28nm CMOS.
nv: Cross-injection-locking mechanism that suppresses jitter in injection-locked oscillators for burst-mode operation.

mx.other: 60Gb/s throughput

t: 31.1 An Inductor-Less Capacitor-Less Synchronous Piezoelectric-Electromagnetic Hybrid Energy Harvesting Platform with Coil-Sharing Scheme

t: Distributed-HISQ: A Distributed Quantum Control Architecture
pb: Distributed quantum control architectures (DQCAs) for superconducting qubits face two blockers: existing lock-step synchronization schemes incur large execution overheads (idle time or full program broadcast across controllers), and existing quantum ISAs are either too high-level or too hardware-specific to support diverse qubit technologies and gate implementation strategies on a single microarchitecture.
me: Distributed-HISQ comprises two mechanisms: (1) HISQ, a hardware instruction set built as an extension to RISC-V 32I that abstracts quantum control as 'send codeword X to port Y at time T,' decoupling instruction semantics from both quantum-operation meaning and analog electronics; and (2) BISP (Booking-based Instruction Synchronization Protocol), which exploits the deterministic duration of quantum gates to pre-book synchronization points in advance, achieving zero-cycle overhead when the deterministic tasks preceding sync are long enough to hide inter-controller communication latency. The system uses a hybrid tree+mesh network topology, with a balanced tree for region-level remote sync and mesh-like intra-layer links mirroring qubit device topology for nearest-neighbor sync. BISP hardware costs only 13 LUTs per SyncU on an FPGA.
nv: The booking-based synchronization protocol (BISP) allows controllers to pre-announce their synchronization time-points before reaching them, eliminating the round-trip latency overhead of prior on-demand sync schemes and enabling zero-cycle synchronization overhead in the common case.

t: SMX: Heterogeneous Architecture for Universal Sequence Alignment Acceleration

The ISA extension adds new instructions to handle variable-length sequences and edge cases, while the coprocessor accelerates the systolic-style inner-loop wavefront computation. Both components support multiple sequence types (DNA, protein, ASCII) and alignment models including weighted affine gap penalties and full substitution matrices, enabling seamless integration with state-of-the-art software alignment algorithms. Physical design targets a 22nm technology node with an area of 0.34mm², 30% of a single-issue in-order CPU core.

t: RTGS: Real-Time 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM via Multi-Level Redundancy Reduction
pb: 3D Gaussian Splatting-based SLAM systems cannot achieve real-time throughput (>=30 FPS) on edge devices; even the most efficient 3DGS-SLAM algorithms run at 0.78–14 FPS on a state-of-the-art edge GPU (NVIDIA ONX). The rendering and backpropagation stages dominate runtime (>80%), with severe workload imbalance across pixels and costly atomic gradient aggregation causing memory conflicts.
me: RTGS is an algorithm-hardware co-design framework targeting 3DGS-SLAM. On the algorithm side: (1) adaptive Gaussian pruning progressively removes low-importance Gaussians by reusing gradients from the backpropagation pass (no added overhead for importance scoring), and (2) dynamic downsampling reduces non-keyframe resolution from 1/16 to 1/4 of full resolution based on temporal distance to nearest keyframe, reusing keyframe identification and alpha-computing results. On the hardware side, a plug-in ASIC integrated alongside edge GPU SMs includes: (1) a Workload Scheduling Unit (WSU) combining pixel-level pairwise scheduling with subtile-level streaming, exploiting inter-iteration workload similarity to reuse scheduling patterns; (2) a Rendering & Backpropagation (R&B) Buffer that stores forward-pass intermediate values (accumulated transmittance T and per-Gaussian color contributions) to eliminate recomputation during backpropagation, reducing alpha gradient latency from 20 to 4 cycles; and (3) a Gradient Merging Unit (GMU) using a Benes network and bypass-extended reduction tree to perform pipelined sparse gradient aggregation, replacing atomic-add operations with structured in-order merging. The design is implemented at 28 nm, 500 MHz, 8.11 W, 28.41 mm2.
nv: Exploiting inter-iteration workload similarity in SLAM (where Gaussians are fixed between tracking iterations) to amortize scheduling overhead across iterations, enabling lightweight pixel-level pairwise scheduling that approaches oracle load balance with negligible cost.

t: Accurate Leakage Speculation for Quantum Error Correction
pb: Physical qubits in quantum error correction (QEC) can leak into higher energy states (e.g., |2>), corrupting syndrome measurements and spreading errors to neighboring qubits; detecting leakage on data qubits is especially hard because they are never directly measured during QEC cycles.
me: GLADIATOR frames leakage detection as a graph labeling problem. Offline, it constructs a code-aware error-propagation graph whose nodes are syndrome patterns and weighted directed edges represent transition probabilities under leakage vs. non-leakage errors, calibrated to device characterization data. Each node accumulates incoming leakage-edge weights (W_L) and non-leakage-edge weights (W_NL); nodes where W_L > W_NL by a threshold factor are labeled as leakage patterns and compiled into a lookup table. Online, a parity-adjacency generator extracts a 5-bit syndrome pattern per data qubit each QEC cycle and a combinational sequence checker (at most 10 LUTs per data qubit) classifies it in under 1 ns, triggering an LRC only for patterns flagged as leakage-dominated. GLADIATOR-D extends the design to a two-round sliding window of syndrome history for further accuracy. The method generalizes to surface codes, color codes, and qLDPC codes.
nv: A probabilistic graph-labeling framework that distinguishes leakage-induced syndrome patterns from standard Pauli-error patterns using calibrated transition probabilities, enabling code-agnostic, low-overhead leakage speculation that requires at most 10 LUTs per data qubit versus 177-5393 LUTs for prior work.

mx.other: 17x-63x FPGA LUT reduction vs. eraser across code distances 5-25; combinational logic evaluates in <1 ns

t: Flexing RISC-V Instruction Subset Processors to Extreme Edge
pb: Extreme edge applications (smart labels, wearable healthcare, smart textiles) require processors that are ultra-low area, ultra-low power, conformable, and low-cost—properties that conventional silicon RISC-V processors and existing smallest designs like Serv cannot meet—while still supporting programmability for occasional firmware updates.

A single-cycle non-pipelined microarchitecture suffices for kHz-range extreme edge performance requirements. For long-lasting applications needing firmware updates, a generative AI tool rewrites instructions not in the subset using equivalent subset instructions.
nv: A bottom-up RISSP generation methodology built on a library of formally pre-verified instruction-granularity RTL blocks, enabling automated generation of minimal-area FlexIC processors without conventional design-and-verify cycles for each new application.

t: REACT3D: Real-time Edge Accelerator for Incremental Training in 3D Gaussian Splatting based SLAM Systems

At the architectural level, a Content Addressable Memory (CAM)-based Dual-index Gaussian Buffer resolves discontinuous memory accesses by maintaining two parallel indices into the Gaussian buffer, avoiding computation conflicts during gradient merging across scattered Gaussian-to-pixel mappings.

t: Towards Closing the Performance Gap for Cryptographic Kernels Between CPUs and Specialized Hardware
pb: Achieving near-ASIC performance for cryptographic kernels (Number Theoretic Transform, NTT; and large-integer BLAS operations) on commodity x86 CPUs remains an open challenge; current CPU baselines lag ASICs by orders of magnitude for these workloads, which are foundational to post-quantum cryptography and fully homomorphic encryption (FHE).
